extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, actors, critics, and cultivated readers interested in drama, comedy, and stage manners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for writing and staging tragedy and comedy (what to show or hide onstage, how to provoke pity or laughter, audience etiquette, and character/devices that produce comic effect).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of children to evoke pity
rubrics_metrics.description: A disconsolate Mother, with a Child in her Hand, has frequently drawn Compassion from the Audience... a Modern Writer ... brought a Princess upon the Stage with a little Boy in one Hand and a Girl in the other ... a third Poet ... introduced three Children, with great Success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such incidents can be beautiful in a good writer but become ridiculous when overused or handled badly: "Thus several Incidents that are beautiful in a good Writer, become ridiculous by falling into the Hands of a bad one." Use sparingly and with tasteful restraint to avoid sentimentality or absurdity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid onstage displays of excessive violence/butchery
rubrics_metrics.description: There is none so absurd and barbarous ... than that dreadful butchering of one another, which is so very frequent upon the English Stage. To delight in seeing Men stabbed, poysoned, racked, or impaled, is certainly the Sign of a cruel Temper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive depiction of stabbing, poison, torture, etc., affronts decency and can brand a people as delighting in blood. Prefer to remove such butcheries from public view; consider telling, implying, or transacting murders offstage rather than showing graphic violence to the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe Horace's rule: avoid representing parricides and unnatural murders before the audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Horace's Rule, expressed in lines such as 'Let not Medea draw her murth'ring Knife, And spill her Children's Blood upon the Stage,' forbids certain kinds of murders (parricides, unnatural horrors) being represented publicly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ancients were sparing of public executions; such acts often have more effect when transacted behind the scenes and related by speech or sounds. Follow the spirit of Horace: banish murders of excessive horror from sight rather than banishing all deaths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer offstage execution and evocative offstage dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: In Sophocles' Orestes the dreadful resolution is executed behind the Scenes: The Mother is heard calling out to her Son for Mercy; and the Son answering her... we find that she is slain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An offstage dialogue or the sounds of violence can be more affecting and plausible than a spectacle of killing. Use reported action, cries, and subsequent presentation of the corpse to preserve decency and increase emotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid improbability and unnaturalness in onstage killings
rubrics_metrics.description: It is very odd, to see our Stage strowed with Carcasses in the last Scene of a Tragedy ... in Corneille's Horatii the hero follows his Sister the whole length of the Stage, and forbears killing her till they are both withdrawn behind the Scenes... it appears very unnatural, and looks like killing in cold Blood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Killings staged in ways that violate probability or natural sentiment (e.g., deliberate walks across the stage to kill) look absurd. If an act would seem implausible or indecent when shown, it should be related, not enacted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy permits broader licence: employ props, costume, and exaggeration
rubrics_metrics.description: Ridicule is not so delicate as Compassion ... there is a much greater Latitude for comick than tragick Artifices ... Bullock in a short Coat, and Norris in a long one, seldom fail of this Effect. In ordinary Comedies, a broad and a narrow brim'd Hat are different Characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy can rely on visual contrasts, costume, physical exaggeration, and simple mechanical jests. Such devices are more indulgible than tragic horrors, but should still serve character and wit rather than only cheap effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience etiquette: preserve silence and decorum during performances
rubrics_metrics.description: A little before the rising of the Curtain, she broke out into a loud Soliloquy ... she asked a Lady ... shook her Fan ... called out to a young Baronet by his Name ... fixed the Attention of all about her. But as I had a mind to hear the Play, I got out of the Sphere of her Impertinence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audience members should not interrupt, call out, whisper loudly, or otherwise draw attention away from the performance. Such impertinence spoils the play for others and is a mark of bad breeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modesty and discretion as ornaments of the fair sex; avoid affectations of travel/french fopperies
rubrics_metrics.description: Discretion and Modesty, which in all other Ages and Countries have been regarded as the greatest Ornaments of the Fair Sex, are considered as the Ingredients of narrow Conversation... The whole Discourse and Behaviour of the French is to make the Sex more Fantastical ... To speak Loud in Publick Assemblies ... are looked upon as Parts of a refined Education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In manners and theatrical representation, guard natural sprightliness from degenerating into levity or immodesty. Fashionable affectations that prize public exposure, loudness, or sham refinement should be censured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory of laughter (Hobbes): laughter arises from comparative superiority
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The Passion of Laughter is nothing else but sudden Glory arising from some sudden Conception of some Eminency in ourselves by Comparison with the Infirmity of others ... For Men laugh at the Follies of themselves past, when they come suddenly to Remembrance.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To provoke laughter, present follies, errors, or infirmities that allow the audience to feel (briefly) superior. Recognize different audiences: coarse tastes laugh at obvious inferiority; refined audiences require more subtle provocatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of comic figures and how they provoke mirth
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a Set of merry Drolls ... those circumforaneous Wits ... always appear in a Fool's Coat, and commit such Blunders and Mistakes ... A particular sort of Men ... I mean, those honest Gentlemen that are always exposed to the Wit and Raillery of their Well-wishers ... stand as Butts in Conversation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic characters may be (a) broad 'merry drolls' who live in folly and physical blunder, or (b) 'butts' in conversation who grant others material for wit. A successful 'butt' often has wit and vivacity so the interplay remains entertaining; a merely stupid butt suits only coarse company.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit pratical joking to appropriate occasions (April Fools vs. daily 'biters')
rubrics_metrics.description: This Art of Wit is well enough, when confined to one Day in a Twelvemonth; but there is an ingenious Tribe of Men sprung up of late Years, who are for making April Fools every Day in the Year. These Gentlemen ... are perpetually employed in laughing at those Mistakes which are of their own Production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pranks and manufactured follies (making others 'fools') are tolerable as occasional diversions (e.g., April Fools); making them habitual cheapens wit and becomes wearisome. Use sparingly to retain effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: A writer's skill distinguishes beautiful incidents from ridiculousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Thus several Incidents that are beautiful in a good Writer, become ridiculous by falling into the Hands of a bad one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical devices (children to provoke pity, staged fright, props for comedy) are neutral; their success depends on the practitioner's taste, restraint, and execution. Avoid slavish copying of effects without craftsmanship.
